## Labor Relations and Collective Bargaining {.section-slide data-background-color="#102a43"}

## Federal Bargaining Rights, by Executive Order

:::: {.timeline .lr-eo}
<div class="tl-step accent-step"><span class="tl-year">March 27, 2025</span><span class="card-heading">Executive Order 14251</span><p>Excludes most federal agencies from collective bargaining, citing national security</p></div>
<div class="tl-step fragment"><span class="tl-year">2025</span><span class="card-heading">Unions sue</span><p>A district court blocks the order; agencies stop honoring contracts where they can</p></div>
<div class="tl-step fragment"><span class="tl-year">Feb. 26, 2026</span><span class="card-heading">Ninth Circuit</span><p>Lifts the injunction. The order is "grounded in national security"; the lawsuit goes on</p></div>
::::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
If a president can end bargaining by executive order, what does a union contract in government protect?
:::

::: source-line
Exec. Order No. 14251, Exclusions from Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs (Mar. 27, 2025); *AFGE v. Trump* (9th Cir. Feb. 26, 2026).
:::

## Unions Are Strongest in Government

::: {.stat-row}
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-number">32.9%</span><p>of public-sector workers are union members</p></div>
<div class="stat fragment"><span class="stat-number">5.9%</span><p>of private-sector workers are</p></div>
<div class="stat fragment"><span class="stat-number">37.8%</span><p>in local government: teachers, police, firefighters</p></div>
:::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Why are the most unionized public employees the ones on the front line?
:::

::: source-line
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Union Members — 2025 (Feb. 18, 2026).
:::

## Three Legal Regimes

::::::: {.system-cols .lr-regimes}
::: system-col
[Private and nonprofit]{.card-heading}

<p>National Labor Relations Act (1935)</p>
<p>Enforced by the NLRB</p>
<p>Right to strike</p>
:::

::: system-col
[Federal]{.card-heading}

<p>Civil Service Reform Act (1978)</p>
<p>Enforced by the FLRA</p>
<p>No strikes; pay set by law, not bargained</p>
:::

::: {.system-col .lr-idaho}
[State and local]{.card-heading}

<p>Each state decides</p>
<p>**Idaho:** right-to-work (1985); bargaining for firefighters and teachers; none for state agency employees</p>
:::
:::::::

::: {.jd-note .fragment}
*Janus v. AFSCME* (2018): no government employer may collect fees from employees who don't join the union.
:::

## How Public-Sector Labor Law Got Here

:::: {.timeline .lr-tl}
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1912</span><span class="card-heading">Lloyd–La Follette</span><p>Federal employees may join employee organizations</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1935</span><span class="card-heading">Wagner Act</span><p>Private-sector right to organize and bargain; creates the NLRB</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1947</span><span class="card-heading">Taft–Hartley</span><p>Bans the closed shop; lets states pass right-to-work laws</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1962</span><span class="card-heading">EO 10988</span><p>Kennedy lets federal employees bargain</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1978</span><span class="card-heading">CSRA</span><p>Puts federal bargaining in statute; creates the FLRA</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1981</span><span class="card-heading">PATCO</span><p>Reagan fires about 11,000 striking air traffic controllers</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">2018</span><span class="card-heading">*Janus*</span><p>Ends agency fees in government</p></div>
<div class="tl-step accent-step"><span class="tl-year">2025</span><span class="card-heading">EO 14251</span><p>Excludes most federal agencies from bargaining</p></div>
::::

## Do We Still Need Unions in Government?

::::: {.compare .jd .roomy .jd-cols}
::: compare-side
[For]{.card-heading}

- A voice for employees in decisions about their work
- Clear, written rules for discipline and promotion
- A check on favoritism and political firing
:::

::: {.compare-side .accent .fragment}
[Against]{.card-heading}

- "Management" is the public: officials bargain with groups that help elect them
- Less flexibility to assign, reward, and discipline
- Civil service law already protects employees
:::
:::::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Where do you stand as an employee? As a manager?
:::

## Collective Bargaining in Three Steps

:::::::::: {.pathway .lr-path}
::: pathway-step
[1. Unit determination]{.card-heading}

<p>Which employees share a "community of interest," and which union represents them</p>
:::

::: pathway-arrow
→
:::

::: pathway-step
[2. Negotiation]{.card-heading}

<p>Scope: mandatory, permissive, and prohibited subjects. Some decisions stay management rights</p>
:::

::: pathway-arrow
→
:::

::: {.pathway-step .accent-step}
[3. Administration]{.card-heading}

<p>Living with the contract: grievances, and labor-management partnerships</p>
:::
::::::::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Most of the work happens in step 3, during the years the contract is in force.
:::

## When Talks Stall: Impasse

:::::::::: {.pathway .lr-path}
::: pathway-step
[Mediation]{.card-heading}

<p>A neutral helps the two sides find a deal. Not binding</p>
:::

::: pathway-arrow
→
:::

::: pathway-step
[Fact-finding]{.card-heading}

<p>A neutral reviews the facts and writes recommendations. Not binding</p>
:::

::: pathway-arrow
→
:::

::: {.pathway-step .accent-step}
[Arbitration]{.card-heading}

<p>A neutral decides. Binding; sometimes "final offer," choosing one side's proposal</p>
:::
::::::::::

::: {.jd-note .fragment}
Strikes: federal employees may not strike. State and local rules vary.
:::

## Grievances: Where the Contract Meets Fairness

:::::::::: {.pathway .lr-path .lr-griev}
::: pathway-step
[Employee and steward]{.card-heading}

<p>Raise it with the supervisor</p>
:::

::: pathway-arrow
→
:::

::: pathway-step
[Department head]{.card-heading}

<p>A written appeal, on a deadline</p>
:::

::: pathway-arrow
→
:::

::: pathway-step
[Top management]{.card-heading}

<p>HR or the agency head</p>
:::

::: pathway-arrow
→
:::

::: {.pathway-step .accent-step}
[A neutral]{.card-heading}

<p>An arbitrator or hearing officer decides</p>
:::
::::::::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Tonight's case is decided at the last step.
:::

## Fair and Inclusive Workplaces {.section-slide data-background-color="#102a43"}

## What Makes a Workplace Fair?

::: big-question
Think of a decision at work that felt unfair. Was it the outcome, the way it was made, or the way you were treated?
:::

## Organizational Justice

::::::: {.system-grid .roomy-grid .lr-justice}
::: system-item
[Distributive]{.card-heading}

<p>Are outcomes, like pay, promotions, and assignments, allocated fairly?</p>
:::

::: {.system-item .fragment}
[Procedural]{.card-heading}

<p>Is the process used to reach them fair and consistent?</p>
:::

::: {.system-item .fragment}
[Interactional]{.card-heading}

<p>Is the decision explained, and are people treated with respect?</p>
:::
:::::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
People accept decisions they don't like when they believe the process was fair.
:::

## Due Process, Revisited

::::: {.compare .jd .roomy .jd-cols}
::: compare-side
[Substantive due process]{.card-heading}

<p>Government can't take life, liberty, or property without good reason</p>
:::

::: compare-side
[Procedural due process]{.card-heading}

<p>Notice, an explanation, a chance to respond, and an explained decision</p>
:::
:::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
*Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill* (1985): a public employee with a property right in the job gets a hearing **before** termination.
:::

## Equal Employment Opportunity Law

:::: {.timeline .lr-tl}
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1963</span><span class="card-heading">Equal Pay Act</span><p>Equal pay for substantially equal work</p></div>
<div class="tl-step accent-step"><span class="tl-year">1964</span><span class="card-heading">Title VII</span><p>Race, color, religion, sex, national origin</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1967</span><span class="card-heading">ADEA</span><p>Age, 40 and over</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1973</span><span class="card-heading">Rehabilitation Act</span><p>Disability, in federal employment and contracts</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1978</span><span class="card-heading">Pregnancy Discrimination Act</span><p>Pregnancy and childbirth</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1990</span><span class="card-heading">ADA</span><p>Disability, extended to state, local, and private employers</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">2008</span><span class="card-heading">GINA</span><p>Genetic information</p></div>
::::

## Two Kinds of Sexual Harassment

::::: {.compare .jd .roomy .jd-cols}
::: compare-side
[Quid pro quo]{.card-heading}

<p>A job benefit is tied to submitting to sexual conduct</p>
:::

::: {.compare-side .accent}
[Hostile work environment]{.card-heading}

<p>Conduct severe or pervasive enough to change the conditions of work</p>
:::
:::::

::: {.jd-note .fragment}
*Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson* (1986): sexual harassment is sex discrimination under Title VII.
:::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Does it matter whether the harasser meant it?
:::

## What the Employer Has to Have in Place

:::::::::: {.pathway .lr-path .lr-employer}
::: pathway-step
[A policy]{.card-heading}

<p>Written, and communicated</p>
:::

::: pathway-arrow
→
:::

::: pathway-step
[Training]{.card-heading}

<p>Especially for supervisors</p>
:::

::: pathway-arrow
→
:::

::: pathway-step
[Ways to report]{.card-heading}

<p>Including one that bypasses the supervisor</p>
:::

::: pathway-arrow
→
:::

::: {.pathway-step .accent-step}
[Prompt action]{.card-heading}

<p>Investigate, discipline in proportion, no retaliation</p>
:::
::::::::::

::: {.jd-note .fragment}
*Faragher v. City of Boca Raton* and *Burlington Industries v. Ellerth* (1998): these steps are the employer's defense when a supervisor harasses.
:::

## Activity: The List {.activity-slide data-background-color="#176b87"}

::: activity-prompt
You work in HR for a mid-sized city. Your best friend works for the city too, is about to have a baby, and closes on a new house in 45 days.
:::

::: activity-prompt
A memo from the city manager lists the employees who will be let go in a reduction in force over the next 30 days. Your friend is on it.
:::

::: jd-questions
1.  Do you tell your friend?
2.  Which kind of justice is at stake: for your friend, and for everyone else on the list?
:::

::: activity-close
5 minutes with a neighbor, then a show of hands
:::

## Bringing It Together

::::: {.compare .jd .roomy .jd-cols}
::: compare-side
[Labor relations]{.card-heading}

- Bargaining in good faith
- Grievance procedures
- A neutral at the end
:::

::: compare-side
[Fair workplaces]{.card-heading}

- Organizational justice
- Due process
- EEO law and harassment policy
:::
:::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Both chapters are about the same thing: a fair process, so that decisions people dislike still hold.
:::
